## Setting up the wiki 

This project's goals have been twofold: to design a VAWT, but also to learn and document where and how agentic tools can assist in the learning and designing process. In this process we first learned how to use new tools such as Opencode, VScode, Obsidian, and GitHub. The first week was therefore not spent researching VAWTs but rather experimenting and learning about these new tools.  

We completed a short workshop for creating a LLM wiki, learned enough GitHub to work in one shared repository, and designed baseline rules for the wiki to fine-tune it for our project. We continued to add to and refine these rules throughout the project, ensuring the LLM relied solely on project sources, would cite its claims, and would label unsupported material. We built an evaluation loop with questions made to intentionally target common fail points of LLMs such as unfounded claims, hallucinations, or sycophancy to test the LLM instead of assuming that an answer which sounded right was reliable. We wanted not to hand off our judgment to an LLM, but to create a source-grounded workspace that could help us find and sort information, locate gaps, and answer technical questions.  

The real setup work came when we started feeding research into the system. We created a workflow to convert PDFs of research papers we gathered into Markdown files while preserving figures and equations. We defined the organization of our wiki pages around concepts, methods, designs, and parameters to create a well-structured database of reliable information. We selected valuable parameters---such as cut-in speed, efficiency, and rated speed--and had the LLM generate metadata for our wiki's design pages to better sort and rank designs within Obsidian. 

![233](data:image/png;base64,)

We had to respond to problems like missing images, poor formatting, unwanted edits to source text, slow or inconsistent runs, and broken links. We addressed these problems by tightening the defined skills, splitting detailed procedures into separate schema documents, and adding Python-based image extractions. All of these efforts went toward creating a tool that can synthesize material quickly and generate fast summarizations of complex problems. The most time-consuming part was not actually asking questions about turbines. It was creating a source we could trust. We have found, however, that with this tool we must be more intentional with our goal of learning, as it can be easy to use it as an answering machine rather than a teacher. It is tempting to skip the slower learning that engineering requires. The value of the wiki has come from treating it as an evolving research process and teaching tool, not as an expert whose first answer should always be accepted. Since it has been trained on only material we sourced, it has become a much more reliable and refined resource than a general chatbot like Chat GPT or Gemini could be for this project.

## Design Goal

In order to narrow down our design space and ensure realistic simulations were performed, we opted to select a specific location for our proposed VAWT. To capitalize on the unique benefits of VAWTs we were looking for urban or suburban locations with moderate wind speeds and a demand for renewable energy. However, our primary concern for selecting a site was that it should have readily accessible wind data that was acquired in a location where we could theoretically install our VAWT. For these reasons, we considered several airports in eastern Massachusetts at which wind data has been collected roughly every minute for many years. Ultimately, we chose Boston Logan International Airport because of its accessible, high-resolution wind data and its average wind speed of about 5 m/s. Additionally, we identified the airport as a high energy demand location with an interest in renewable energy since the Massachusetts Department of Transportation intends to reach net-zero emissions by 2028.

Before moving forward with BOS we needed to ensure it would be possible to install our VAWT on the premises, ideally as close as possible to the location at which the wind data is collected in the center of the airfield about 9 m from the ground. We utilized the LLM to read through the Federal Aviation Administration regulations about construction in and around airports and determined that Governor's Island, an outer section of the airfield that faces the bay on two sides, includes at least 10 acres of VAWT-compatible space.

![360](data:image/png;base64,)

With a location selected, our next step was to analyze the wind data and determine what criteria our design should meet in order to perform optimally in the particular wind conditions on Governor's Island. We added two years of wind data to the wiki and used the LLM to generate a histogram of the data, sorting it by wind speed. 

![290](data:image/png;base64,)

The LLM was also able to quickly analyze the data and, with its access to information about VAWT performance, helped us determine what design parameters we should aim for in order to design a VAWT that would take full advantage of the available wind power at BOS.

  

## Concept Selection Process 

After defining our design goal we moved onto the concept selection phase to determine which VAWT designs or concepts in the wiki would be best suited to use as a starting point for optimization. To begin narrowing the list of 63 VAWT designs in the wiki, we each selected 8-10 promising designs based on their perceived potential for efficacy at BOS and if they were interesting concepts to pursue, with the help of the LLM. After comparing our initial design selections, we agreed upon six designs to evaluate further. A list of selection criteria was developed based on our design goal, and used to score these potential VAWT designs. The criteria used were "Startup ability" (with a goal of <= 3 m/s), "Efficiency," "Rated speed" (goal: 10-15 m/s), "Cut-out speed" (goal: <= 20 m/s), "Room for Growth" (indicating potential to iterate upon the design), "CAD & Manufacturing Feasibility," and "Team Interest". First, we each manually scored the designs before asking the LLM to repeat the exercise. The human and LLM scores were very similar for most categories, especially for quantitative criteria. The LLM scores for qualitative criteria such as difficulty to model in CAD software or interest in pursuing, were replaced with the average of our scores. After scoring, we weighted the criteria based on their importance to our design goal and project feasibility, and ranked the designs.

![365](data:image/png;base64,)

In order to perform a sensitivity analysis of our scores and weights, we prompted the LLM to rank the designs using three different weighting schemes based on different 'personas'. These were a beginner/student engineer with minimal CAD or CFD experience, an expert engineer with extensive CAD and CFD experience, and an engineer whose primary goal was simply to produce the most optimal VAWT for BOS, regardless of constraints. After ranking the six selected designs with these weights the same two designs repeatedly came out on top, validating our selection process. This sensitivity test also helped make clear the relative strengths and weaknesses of the top two designs which further informed our next steps. Before moving on we used the LLM to apply the ranking system to all 63 designs in the wiki to ensure that our initial pass hadn't prematurely eliminated any designs. We found that H-type VAWT designs made up a large proportion of the top-ranked designs with the previously identified best designs remaining the top two. The two designs selected to move forward were a dual-phase H-type VAWT, and a unique Darrieus VAWT, pictured below. In order to decide which of the two designs to begin testing, both were moved forward into the CAD phase to gauge modeling feasibility.

The use of AI significantly accelerated the process of reviewing research papers and assessing VAWT designs. The LLM could quickly retrieve and compare information across the entire wiki which was extremely helpful for both human-driven design exploration and for AI-driven filters and rankings. AI helped identify candidate concepts, extract structured design data, compile comparison tables, and calculate weighted scores. This made it possible to go from a large set of designs to selecting two within a single afternoon. However, after having completed this process we noticed that the efficiency cost us the deep learning that can really only be achieved through time spent directly engaging with the material. For this reason we endeavored to take advantage of the quick information retrieval capabilities of the LLM while remaining actively involved in manually assessing top designs and using our own judgement to structure the process and review all LLM recommendations. This was also essential to ensure that the work done by AI was fully accurate, especially when sources were less clear about their outcomes or reported them primarily through figures.

  

## CAD

After selecting the most promising designs, we began modeling them with CAD software. As per the AI-exploration objective of this project, we explored two AI CAD tools: Zoo Design Studio's Zookeeper, and Fusion's Autodesk Assistant. We used the LLM wiki to generate prompts for the CAD AI agents based on the design specifications in the research papers for the two selected VAWT designs. The dual-phase H-type design was very well described so the AI prompt was quite robust and very successful. The unique Darrieus design provided more of a prompting challenge due to a lack of design specifications in the source paper. We found that shorter, more constrained prompts worked better than the long-winded prompts that the LLM initially produced. After the first prompt there were often some obvious errors such as disconnected blades or floating components, which through both re-prompting and directly editing the KCL code we repaired. The unique Darrieus design was much more difficult to accurately reproduce due to incomplete geometry specifications. The source provided the overall rotor dimensions and described the inward, cup-like blade ends, but it did not provide us with information on blade profile or many structural dimensions. The dual-phase H-type design provided complete geometric specifications for the turbine blades. The specific detail made this design a stronger option for modeling, but still it was not error-free. ZooKeeper created disconnected blades, floating parts, and missing struts when asked for edits with increased detail. Fusion gave us a faster model that looked more accurate than ZooKeeper’s at first, but its inner blades were not the specified airfoil. AI powered CAD tools greatly sped up the modeling process but still required careful editing to correctly assemble the model.
